notes:
I found good verse-by-verse material for most of the chapter, but there are clear gaps, which I list at the end. Several verses have no notes at all.

# Romans 11: Research Notes

## 1. What the commentators say, verse by verse

**v. 1:** Guzik says Paul is asking whether Israel's fate is now settled with no hope of restoration, given that rejecting the gospel was both consistent with God's eternal plan (Romans 9:1-29) and Israel's own choosing (Romans 9:30-10:21). His answer is that Paul himself is the evidence: Paul's faith in Jesus as the Messiah proved there were some Jews chosen by God who embraced the gospel. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-11/

**v. 2:** According to the BibleHub summary, the Greek word for "foreknew" (proegnō) implies God's foreknowledge and intimate relationship with Israel. — https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/romans/11.htm
Guzik notes that things were bad enough for Elijah to pray against his own people. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-11/

**vv. 3–4:** Elijah thought that God had cast off the nation and he was the only one left serving the Lord. But God showed him that there was in fact a substantial remnant – though it was only a remnant, it was actually there. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-11/

**v. 5:** Guzik's lesson is that God often works through a small group. Though not many Jews in Paul's day embraced Jesus as Messiah, a remnant did and God will use that small group in a big way. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-11/
The Greek word for remnant (leimma) means a small amount left over, which points to God keeping a faithful group. — https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/romans/11.htm

**v. 6:** Guzik defines grace as God's free gift. It is not given with an eye to what the receiver might do. It comes only from the giver's kindness. Grace and works, as principles, cannot be mixed. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-11/

**vv. 7–10:** Guzik says the elect in Israel responded to God's mercy, and the rest were hardened by their own rejection. The quotations from Isaiah 29 and Psalm 69 show that God may enlighten only a remnant for now if He chooses. Leon Morris calls the "spirit of stupor" a deadness toward spiritual things. William Barclay explains the "table" (v. 9) as a feast where people feel so safe that their sense of safety becomes their ruin. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-11/

**v. 11:** Guzik separates stumbling from falling. Israel stumbled, but did not fall in the sense of being removed from God's plan. He adds that the gospel often went to the Gentiles only after Jews rejected it (Acts 13:46; 18:5–6; 28:25–28). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-11/

**v. 12:** Guzik writes that Israel's rejection did not itself cause Gentiles to be saved. It opened more opportunity for the gospel to reach them, and many took it. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-11/

**vv. 13–14:** Paul hopes for a good kind of jealousy that would draw Jews to the blessings Gentiles now enjoy. Guzik quotes Morris's regret that Christians have mostly treated Jews with hatred and persecution instead of making them envious of the faith. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-11/

**v. 15:** John Piper (Baptist) reads the parallel this way: The nation now rejected will be accepted. So the "acceptance" of the Jewish nation most naturally refers to the salvation of "all Israel" — the salvation of the nation as a whole some day. — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/all-israel-will-be-saved

**v. 16:** Guzik takes the "firstfruit" to be the first Jewish Christians. He notes that many commentators take the firstfruit here as the patriarchs, but thinks the first group of believers fits better. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-11/
The BibleHub summary instead says the holy roots are the patriarchs. — https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/romans/11.htm

**v. 17:** Guzik quotes Morris: in the ancient world, one cure for a weak old olive tree was to graft in wild shoots. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-11/
Ryrie and MacArthur, quoted on Precept Austin, say the root is the covenant God made with Abraham. Ryrie calls the tree the place of privilege first held by the natural branches. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_1116-18
Matthew Henry takes the tree to be the visible church. He says Abraham was its root, while Christ alone is the root that gives life. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rom/Rom_011.cfm

**vv. 18–21:** Paul warns Gentile believers against spiritual pride three times (vv. 18, 20, 25). They were no better than the Jews, but were grafted into the tree by God's grace alone. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_1116-18
Guzik notes that Gentiles stand in the tree by faith alone, and they too will be cut off if they do not believe. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-11/

**v. 22:** Guzik says "continue in His goodness" does not mean salvation by works. It means an ongoing abiding in God's grace, like John 15. He quotes John Murray that there is no security in the gospel apart from perseverance. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-11/

**vv. 23–24:** Gill (Baptist) points out that grafting a wild shoot into a good tree goes against normal practice, so this grafting is pure grace. If God did that for Gentiles, it is even more likely He will bring the natural branches back. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/11-24.html
Henry puts it this way: Men graft to mend the tree; but God grafts to mend the branch. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_1116-18

**v. 25:** Guzik reads "in part" as meaning the blindness is temporary. He also argues that "spiritual Israel" cannot be meant here, because the Israel in this verse is spiritually blind. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-11/

**v. 26:** See section 2 below for the main debate.
Guzik says "all Israel" means the nation as a whole, not every last Jew, and that they will be saved by faith in Jesus. They are not saved with some peculiar "Jewish" salvation. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-11/
Barnes adds that Paul does not say when this will happen. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/11-26.htm

**v. 27:** Precept Austin argues that "My covenant with them" refers, in this context, to God's covenant with ethnic Israel, not the church. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_1117-33

**vv. 28–29:** Guzik says Israel remains "beloved" for the sake of the patriarchs, even though in Paul's day they opposed the gospel. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-11/
On Precept Austin, "irrevocable" (ametamelētos) means God will not change His mind about His promises to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_1128-32
Guzik also applies v. 29 to believers generally while admitting that the original context is Israel. — https://enduringword.com/never-taken-back/

**vv. 30–31:** Bridgeway: just as the Jews were the means of God's mercy going to the Gentiles, so the Gentiles are now the means of his mercy going to the Jews. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/11-32.html

**v. 32:** See section 3 below on universalism.
Barnes and Calvin both stress the word "mercy": God owes no one anything, and everyone is saved freely because everyone is equally lost. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/11-32.html

**vv. 33–36:** Guzik calls this Paul's triumphant conclusion: he thinks about God's plan and breaks into praise. We cannot reach the depth of God's wisdom, but we can rest knowing He has everything in hand. — https://enduringword.com/of-him-through-him-and-to-him/
The BibleHub summary notes that the chapter ends not in argument but adoration. — https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/romans/11.htm

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ

**v. 26: Who is "all Israel"?**
- **Calvin (Reformed):** He applies "Israel" to all God's people, gathered from both Jews and Gentiles, with the Jews returning to faith as part of that whole. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/11-26.html
- **Other older commentators on the same page:** The Pulpit Commentary rejects Calvin's view because "Israel" should mean the same nation it meant in v. 25. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the verse can only mean the ultimate ingathering of Israel as a nation, in contrast with the present "remnant." — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/11-26.html
- **Reformed, TGC:** This article argues for a third view. "All Israel" is the believing Jewish remnant plus the hardened majority, and Gentile inclusion is the means God uses to save them. — https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/israel-saved-romans-11/
- **Baptist, Piper:** A future conversion of the nation as a whole, probably at the second coming. — https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/five-reasons-i-believe-romans-11-26-means-a-future-conversion-for-israel
- **Pentecostal/Calvary Chapel, Guzik:** Ethnic Israel will be saved in the future. He says the passage refutes the view that the church has inherited every promise made to Israel. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-11/
- **Dispensational, GotQuestions:** This view sets literal fulfilment, including the land promise, against "replacement theology." — https://www.gotquestions.org/all-Israel-saved.html
- **Methodist, Wesley and Clarke:** Wesley says Israel will be convinced by seeing the Gentiles come in, followed by an even larger harvest among the Gentiles. Clarke says "saved" means being brought into the way of salvation by accepting the Messiah, not every Jew reaching glory. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/11-26.html
- **Restoration Movement, Coffman:** He takes v. 26 to mean spiritual Israel (Jews and Gentiles together) and sees no promise that Israel's hardening will end. — https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/romans-11.html
- **History of the debate:** BibleHub's overview says Augustine first saw "all Israel" as the church but later spoke of a future turning of the Jews. It adds that Luther and Calvin differed on the timing. — https://biblehub.com/q/Meaning_of_all_Israel_will_be_saved.htm

**v. 22: Can a believer be "cut off"?**
- **Calvin:** Paul is speaking to the Gentiles as a whole body, not to elect individuals. Persevering in faith flows from election itself. — https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/comment3/comm_vol38/htm/xv.v.htm
- **Monergism (Reformed):** The warning is to the visible church as a group. Not every member is actually united to Christ in a saving way. — https://www.monergism.com/blog/do-cut-olive-branches-romans-11-definitively-prove-salvation-can-be-lost
- **Coffman (Restoration Movement, an Arminian-leaning tradition):** Every promise to those saved by grace depends on their continuing, and the warning is addressed to real Christians. — https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/romans-11.html
- **Precept Austin:** It notes the dilemma that if the tree means believing Jews, Paul would seem to teach that salvation can be lost. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_1116-18

## 3. Other views

**Catholic (Haydock's commentary):**
- **vv. 11–15:** Israel's fall is not beyond repair. The Jews are cast off only partly and for a time. — https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/romans-11.html
- **vv. 16–24:** Gentiles are grafted onto the root of the patriarchs and become Abraham's spiritual children by imitating his faith. — https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/romans-11.html
- I only saw a search snippet of this page; the full page would not load.

**Universalism (v. 32):** Piper responds to Thomas Talbott's reading, under which Romans 11 teaches universalism: all individuals will finally be saved. Piper's reply is that the two "alls" mean the full number of Jews and Gentiles as groups. — https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/universalism-in-romans-9-11
Ligonier agrees: Paul means mercy on all *kinds* of people. — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/mercy-all

**Two covenants for Jews and Christians?** Guzik takes up the question of whether Israel could be saved without seeking Jesus. His answer is no: the Spirit will lead them to faith in Christ. — https://enduringword.com/does-romans-1125-32-teach-that-israel-will-be-saved-apart-from-seeking-jesus/
